checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: How should customer events be partitioned to preserve ordering per customer while scaling across partitions?

options.label: Send without a key
options.sub: let the producer distribute events across partitions
options.verdict: This can spread load well, but two events for the same customer may land on different partitions. Kafka does not guarantee topic-wide order, so consumers could observe those customer events out of sequence.

options.label: Key by customer_id
options.sub: route each customer's events to one partition
options.verdict: A stable customer_id key sends that customer's events to the same partition, preserving their partition-local order while other customers are processed in parallel. The tradeoff is hot-key skew: a very active customer can overload one partition.

defend.prompt: Which consequences follow from partitioning and consumer groups?

options.label: Ordering is guaranteed within a partition
Consumer-group parallelism is bounded by partition count
A hot customer can skew load onto one partition
All consumer groups share one committed offset

defend.explain: Kafka orders records within each partition, and one partition can be assigned to only one active consumer in a group, so adding group members beyond the partition count adds no parallelism. A heavily used customer_id can create a hot partition. Separate consumer groups maintain independent offsets, allowing each group to consume or replay the same log at its own pace.

checkpoints.title: Semantics ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Reason from Kafka's ordering, parallelism, and offset semantics.

rungs.note: Offsets define record order inside a partition; Kafka does not provide one total order across a multi-partition topic.

rungs.q: With 12 partitions, how many consumers in one group can actively consume them at once?
rungs.note: Each partition is assigned to one consumer in the group, so a thirteenth consumer has no partition to own.

rungs.q: What happens if a consumer writes output, then crashes before committing its offset?
choices: The output is automatically rolled back
rungs.note: On restart, the consumer resumes from the last committed offset and processes the record again. Kafka cannot automatically undo an external write.

checkpoints.explain: Kafka's default consumer behavior is at-least-once: work completed before an offset commit can be repeated after a crash. Commit after successful output to avoid loss, and make an external sink idempotent or coordinate it transactionally so replay does not duplicate effects.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the durable, ordered path from an event to replay-safe processing.
checkpoints.explain: The producer attaches a key so related events reach one partition, whose leader appends them to its ordered log. In-sync replicas copy the append for durability according to the acknowledgment configuration. A consumer group assigns each partition to one member for parallel processing. A successful sink effect precedes the offset commit, and replay after a pre-commit crash remains safe because the sink is idempotent. Random routing loses per-key ordering, blob payloads misuse Kafka for large data, and committing an offset before work risks loss if the consumer crashes.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: One partition's lag is rising while overall broker and consumer capacity remain healthy. Diagnose the root cause.
checkpoints.explain: The top key carries 62% of traffic, concentrating records on one partition and producing the observed lag. Adding consumers to the same group cannot split that partition because only one group member can own it at a time. Redesign or salt the key only when the ordering requirements permit related events to be distributed across partitions.

wrong.Partition 7: Its 2.4M lag is the symptom and identifies where work accumulated, but the concentrated partition key explains why traffic collected there.
wrong.Broker Network: At 38% utilization, shared broker networking has headroom; a network bottleneck would be expected to affect more than one partition.
wrong.Consumer Fleet: Fleet CPU is only 44%. More consumers might help across partitions, but they cannot divide Partition 7 among multiple members of the same group.
